lines.text: A hook is your own code that runs at a set point in the agent's lifecycle, every time.
No model decides whether it runs.|That makes hooks the only layer that enforces.
Use them for what must always happen: blocking, formatting, logging.
The lifecycle has points like session start, prompt submitted,|before a tool runs, after it runs, and stop.
Claude Code has thirty-three of them.
A hook can be a shell command, an HTTP call, an MCP tool, a prompt, or another agent.
lines.say: A hook can be a shell command, an H T T P call, an M C P tool, a prompt, or another agent.

lines.text: Before a tool runs, a command that exits with code two blocks it.
Each hook receives the event as JSON, like the exact command about to run.
lines.say: Each hook receives the event as JSON, like the exact command about to run.

lines.text: And hooks from every scope all fire. They add up; they don't override.
Run /hooks to see every hook that's configured.
lines.say: Run slash hooks to see every hook that's configured.

lines.text: This one runs before every shell command.
If the command is a force push,|it prints the reason and exits with code two.
The push never happens,|and the agent reads the reason and changes course.
The same pattern can block edits to secrets,|or format a file after every write.
A rule that says never edit .env is a request.|A hook that blocks it is a guarantee.
lines.say: A rule that says never edit dot env is a request. A hook that blocks it is a guarantee.

lines.text: But prove it fires. In the setup behind this series,|the guard hooks sat in an example file and never ran.
Hooks cost no context unless they print something.
Codex has hooks too, in hooks.json, with a smaller set of events.
lines.say: Codex has hooks too, in hooks dot JSON, with a smaller set of events.
